## What You Will Learn

In this mission, you will learn why `SELECT *` is considered an anti-pattern in production databases and how selecting only the columns you need makes queries faster and more maintainable.

### The Problem with SELECT *

When you write `SELECT *`, the database has to:
- Read every column from the table (including large text blobs, JSON, or binary data you don't need)
- Transfer all that data over the network to your application
- Consume more memory in your application layer

Beyond performance, `SELECT *` breaks when:
- A new column is added to the table schema
- A column is renamed or reordered
- Someone adds a `TEXT` or `BLOB` column that wasn't there before

### Key Concepts
- **Explicit column list**: List only the columns you actually need in your `SELECT` clause.
- **Index utilization**: Queries on specific columns can leverage indexes; `SELECT *` often forces full table scans.
- **Schema independence**: Explicit columns protect your code from schema changes.

### The Table We're Using
| Column | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `order_id` | INTEGER | Primary key |
| `customer_id` | INTEGER | Foreign key to customers |
| `order_date` | DATE | When the order was placed |
| `status` | TEXT | Order status (completed, pending, cancelled) |
| `total_amount` | DECIMAL | Order total value |
| `notes` | TEXT | Optional customer notes (can be very large) |

### Why This Matters
In real reporting dashboards and APIs, returning only needed columns reduces latency and memory usage significantly. A query that fetches 20 columns when you only need 3 wastes bandwidth and CPU on every request.
